book.title: The Telegraph All New Toughie Crossword, book 1

clue.text: Taking chances with targets and various other things

parts.note: a gambler taking chances is playing the odds, the prices offered on a bet
with means together, the same job as the joining word and
ends are aims or goals, the things one targets

explanation.surface: A gambler or archer taking risks with targets and assorted other things.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end; the start reads as one phrase but is three pieces strung together.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds and ends is the idiom for miscellaneous leftover items, an assortment of bits and pieces.

clue.text: Item of cattle feed? Muse, picking up one, only half keen

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking up means lifting, so the Muse's name reads upwards

parts.note: Clio is the Muse of history
a, as in one item
the first two of the word's four letters

explanation.surface: A pensive figure considering cattle feed, only half enthusiastic.
explanation.definitionFit: Oilcake is a block of compressed seeds left after oil is pressed out, fed to livestock.

clue.text: Really like vermouth? Here's a finger

parts.note: to dig something is slang for enjoying it
It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: A drinker keen on vermouth offers a finger of it.
explanation.walkthrough: A finger here looks like a measure of drink but is meant literally; gin and It is gin with Italian vermouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Digit is the anatomical term for a finger or toe.

clue.text: Lad embraces daughter after a new year with someone unspecified

indicators.note: the boy and daughter come after the earlier letters

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: holds inside, so the word for lad wraps around the daughter

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A boy hugs a daughter as the new year begins with a mystery guest.
explanation.definitionFit: Anybody means any person at all, one not named or specified.

clue.text: Really serious? It's accepted by King, perhaps facing revolution

indicators.note: about to be turned round, so the whole is read backwards
taken in, so the card's letters close around the first words

parts.note: a king is one example of a playing card
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Is the monarch facing an uprising truly grave?
explanation.walkthrough: King looks like royalty facing a revolt; it is only an example of a card.
explanation.definitionFit: Drastic means severe or extreme in effect, so it fits a very serious situation.

clue.text: Classic silent film of Nature's flickering

indicators.note: moving and wavering, as an old film flickers, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Nature's flickering images make up a classic film of the silent era.
explanation.walkthrough: Flickering suits a silent film projector, so it reads as description.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosferatu, Murnau's 1922 vampire film, is a celebrated classic of the silent cinema.

clue.text: Conflict involved in act to restore clan?

indicators.note: taken inside, so the conflict goes within the proofreading mark

parts.note: stet, let it stand, is the proofreader's mark cancelling a deletion
a war is a conflict

explanation.surface: A war breaks out within a campaign to bring back a Scottish clan.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that this is a royal clan whose restoration really happened, in 1660, as the Stuarts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stewarts are a Scottish clan and royal house, spelt Stuart after the Restoration of the monarchy.

clue.text: Congested pub with cricket side arriving — crikey!

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for public house
leg is the on side of a cricket field, one half of the pitch as seen by the batsman
my! is an exclamation of surprise, like crikey

explanation.surface: A packed bar as the cricket team rolls in, with the drinker gasping in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Congested here is the medical sense: a chest or nose full of mucus. PH is the map abbreviation for a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A phlegmy chest or nose is clogged with mucus, which is what being congested means in illness.

clue.text: Assist with topic that's reinterpreted what gets bird down?

indicators.note: read in a new way, so the letters of the two words take a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Help with a subject seen afresh, about what brings a bird low.
explanation.walkthrough: Down suggests feathers or shooting; here it means ill. The answer is parrot fever, a disease of birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Psittacosis is parrot fever, a bacterial infection that makes birds sick, so it gets them down.

clue.text: Sailor's in contact with waste material in infected spot

indicators.note: touching each other, so the two pieces sit side by side in order

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, with the 's
cess is an old word for sewage, as in cesspit

explanation.surface: A seaman touching filth ends up with an infected sore.
explanation.walkthrough: Cess survives mainly in cesspit and cesspool, a store for waste.
explanation.definitionFit: An abscess is a swollen pocket of pus where tissue has become infected.

clue.text: My sole star's variable (which would do for my planets!)

definitions.text: My sole star's variable (which would do for my planets!)

indicators.note: changeable, so the letters of the first three words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: An astronomer muses that their only sun changes, so the planets around it must too.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as the speech of something with one star and several planets.
explanation.definitionFit: Our own planetary family is the Sun with the planets orbiting it, one star with many worlds.

clue.text: Unsuitable betting selection may be seen in it

indicators.note: says the selection appears inside the next word of the clue

parts.note: taken as written
a nap is a tipster's strongest selection of the day, the horse to bet on

explanation.surface: A poor choice of bet turns up in some unsuitable context.
explanation.walkthrough: A nap, in racing tipsters' columns, is the single best bet of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: Inapt means not appropriate or fitting, so it is a synonym for unsuitable.

clue.text: Exactly where the varnish goes?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: precisely, especially of a payment made promptly
second meaning, taken literally: nail varnish is painted onto the fingernail

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for precise or prompt payment is read literally as the place nail varnish is applied.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means precisely or promptly, from paying cash down on the spot without delay.

clue.text: Go without lace that's ruined with a sticky substance

indicators.note: in the old sense outside, so the word for go wraps around the rest

parts.note: a go is an attempt, a try

indicators.note: the lace is spoilt and its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone giving up a spoilt piece of lace that has been smeared with goo.
explanation.walkthrough: Without is used in its old meaning of outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Treacly describes something coated in or like treacle, a thick sugary syrup that sticks.

clue.text: Heavenly seat I represented in monkish retreat

indicators.note: placed inside the monk's room

parts.note: a cell is a monk's small private room

indicators.note: presented again in another form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A heavenly throne pictured inside a monastery.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay needs an I alongside seat; the book's text has lost it.
explanation.definitionFit: Celestial means belonging to the sky or to heaven, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Caught one often affected by mercury gas

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
hat makers were poisoned by mercury used on felt, hence mad as a hatter

explanation.surface: Someone poisoned by mercury vapour, caught out by the gas.
explanation.walkthrough: Gas is the verb or noun meaning idle talk, not a vapour; Victorian hatters went mad from the mercury used to treat felt.
explanation.definitionFit: To gas is to talk idly at length, which is what chatter means.

clue.text: Fellow with poor service getting honour?

parts.note: a chap is a man, a fellow
in tennis a let is a serve that clips the net and must be replayed

explanation.surface: A tennis player with a weak serve somehow being rewarded.
explanation.walkthrough: A chaplet is a wreath or garland worn on the head, as given to a victor.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplet is a garland for the head, awarded as a mark of distinction like a laurel wreath.

clue.text: Release girl seen around home

indicators.note: the girl's name sits outside the home

parts.note: Amy is a girl's name
a nest is a home

explanation.surface: A girl spotted near her house is set free.
explanation.definitionFit: An amnesty is a general pardon releasing offenders or prisoners from punishment.

clue.text: City enthralling fellow in toto

indicators.note: holding captive, so the last word wraps round the fellow

parts.note: taken as written
Ron, a man's name

explanation.surface: A captivating city that charms a man entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: In toto, Latin for altogether, reads as a phrase but its second word is the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Toronto is Canada's largest city, the capital of Ontario.

clue.text: Gallant Duke, rugged first to last, ending in victory

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for rugged is moved to its end

parts.note: rugged and tough both mean hardy and strong

indicators.note: only the final letter of the following word is used

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A brave, rugged nobleman who comes through to win at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Doughty is an old word for brave and stout-hearted, so it matches gallant in its sense of valiant.

clue.text: Lifting hat to girl's a problematic situation

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising the word means reading it upwards

parts.note: lid is slang for a hat
Emma is a girl's name; the 's is the verb is

explanation.surface: Whether to doff your cap to a girl is a tricky question.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilemma is a quandary, a choice between two unwelcome options.

clue.text: Saxon ruler left out of lively English time

indicators.note: moving about energetically, so the remaining letters are jumbled
taken away from, so the letter for left is dropped from the word after

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An Anglo-Saxon king driven out of a lively bit of English history.
explanation.definitionFit: Hengist, with his brother Horsa, was a legendary leader of the first Saxon settlers in Kent.

clue.text: Crime is leading to court case absolving one of the Left

parts.note: a sin is a wrongdoing, loosely a crime
taken as written

indicators.note: absolving lets one off, so the letter for one is released from the trial

parts.note: a trial is the hearing of a case in court
the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A political story: wrongdoing leads to a trial in which a left-winger is cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L makes the Left look political, but the answer is the Latin-based word for left-handed or on the left side.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinistral means on or towards the left side, from Latin sinister, left.

clue.text: A painter fellow (and French)

parts.note: a man is a fellow
et is French for and

explanation.surface: An artist, his friend, and some French connection.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket reads as an aside, but it is a piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Édouard Manet was a French artist, one example of a painter.

clue.text: Detective is brought in increasingly

indicators.note: placed inside the next word

parts.note: more, as in more and more
the s of the contraction 's

explanation.surface: A detective is called in more and more often.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspector Morse is the Oxford police officer in Colin Dexter's novels and the TV series.

clue.text: Rumours returning about half of S&M period

indicators.note: around, so the reversed word goes round the next piece
going back, so the word for rumours is read in reverse

parts.note: noises are reports or talk, as in making noises about something
one of the two letters of S&M

explanation.surface: Gossip going round about a kinky period in someone's life.
explanation.definitionFit: A session is a stretch of time given to an activity, such as a sitting of a court or a term.

clue.text: Schoolmistress keeping a number back left stuff

indicators.note: holding, so the schoolmistress word goes round the rest

parts.note: marm, short for madam, is a name for a schoolmistress

indicators.note: the number is written backwards

parts.note: six, any number will do and this one fits

explanation.surface: A teacher kept back a number of pupils and left her things behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Left stuff means left-wing ideology, not things left behind; schoolmarm gives the teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Marxism is the socialist doctrine of Karl Marx, the archetype of left-wing political thought.

clue.text: Cry with pain, later collapsing as a warning

parts.note: to yell is to cry out
ow is what one says when hurt

indicators.note: a collapsing word falls into disorder, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shouts in pain, then falls down, as a warning to others.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellow alert is a state of caution, the stage of alarm before a red alert.
